The central question is whether the probability scores a RAG system uses to select documents and the probability scores the generator uses to produce tokens can be composed into a coherent, jointly calibrated signal — and the answer is almost certainly no without explicit intervention. Retrieval scores (BM25 relevance, dense embedding cosine similarity, or learned reranker logits) live in a completely different probability space than the autoregressive token log-probabilities the LM produces; fusing them naively via score interpolation or simple concatenation into the prompt implicitly treats them as commensurate when they are not. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the silent compounding failure mode: when retrieval scores are high but misleading (e.g., a topically similar but factually contradictory document ranks first), the generator doesn't experience epistemic tension — it fluently incorporates the wrong content with high token confidence, and the joint score still looks healthy because both signals are individually high. The expert also worries about score fusion schemes like RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) or linear interpolation of retrieval and generation scores during beam search, which destroy the marginal calibration of each component signal without producing a new well-calibrated composite, giving you a number that feels like a confidence but has undefined probabilistic semantics.

The distributional property formally violated is marginal calibration: a score function s is marginally calibrated if E[Y | s(X) = p] = p; retrieval scores fail this by construction because they are never trained against a binary "does this document contain the correct answer" objective with proper scoring rule loss, and linear interpolation of an uncalibrated score with a miscalibrated log-probability cannot recover marginal calibration — the composite ECE is lower-bounded by a weighted combination of each component's individual miscalibration, with no cancellation term unless the errors are perfectly anti-correlated, which they empirically are not. The failure mode is a latent variable collapse analogous to posterior collapse in VAEs: when the generator (typically a strong seq2seq model like BART or T5-large) becomes capable of producing plausible answers from the question alone — without conditioning on any retrieved document — the ELBO gradient signal to the retriever vanishes because the KL term between the retrieval posterior and prior flattens, and the reconstruction term ∑_z p(z|x) log p(y|x,z) becomes insensitive to which z is selected. Concretely, in RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) the retrieval distribution is approximated as a top-k categorical over DPR scores, and the ELBO marginalizes over this k-document set; if the generator assigns nearly uniform log-likelihood across all k documents (because it can answer without them), the gradient ∂log p(y|x,z)/∂z_scores becomes near-zero, and the DPR encoder receives no meaningful update signal — the retriever freezes at its initialization distribution while the generator fine-tunes away from needing it. This is the RAG-specific manifestation of the "explaining away" problem: the generator explains away the retrieval latent by finding a low-perplexity path through its parametric memory, effectively setting p(y|x,z) ≈ p(y|x) for all z in the retrieved set, which collapses the posterior p(z|x,y) toward the prior p(z|x) and eliminates the training signal that would push the retriever toward factually grounding documents. Empirically, Shuster et al. (2021) in the context of dialogue RAG observed that generator perplexity on gold-retrieved versus randomly-retrieved documents converged during training on knowledge-rich generators, a direct signature of retrieval collapse — the model had learned to ignore the conditioning document. The fix attempted in REALM was asynchronous index refresh with a momentum encoder and an inverse cloaking objective that masked salient spans to force retrieval dependency, but this only works when the generator cannot reconstruct the masked spans from context alone — a condition that fails for sufficiently large generators fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora where parametric memory already covers the target distribution.

Guu et al. Asymmetric updating restructures the bias into two separable components that can be analyzed independently: query-side drift δ_q = ||θ_q^t - θ_q^{t-k}|| and document-side drift δ_d = ||θ_d^t - θ_d^{t-k}||, and the inner product mismatch that determines retrieval ranking error scales as δ_q · δ_d under a first-order Taylor expansion of the cosine similarity — meaning that freezing one encoder while updating the other does not halve the bias but instead eliminates one drift term entirely, leaving only the cross term from the updated encoder's movement against the frozen encoder's fixed geometry. In systems like ColBERT-v2 (Santhanam et al., 2022) and BGE-M3, the document encoder is frozen post-indexing while only the query encoder is fine-tuned at inference-time adaptation, which provably eliminates δ_d from the bias expression and reduces the ELBO staleness bias to a function of query encoder drift alone — this is strictly better than symmetric REALM whenever the query distribution shifts faster than the document distribution, which is the common case in domain adaptation. However, asymmetric updating introduces a new failure mode absent in the symmetric case: representational space fracture, where the query encoder's embedding space rotates or scales relative to the frozen document encoder's space, so that even if query-side drift is small in parameter space, the induced geometric mismatch in embedding space can be large — Khattab & Zaharia (2020) observed this in early ColBERT experiments where fine-tuning the query encoder alone on new domains caused systematic angular drift that degraded MRR@10 by 8-12 points despite low parameter norm change. The bias is provably better than symmetric REALM in expectation when the document corpus is static and the query encoder's learning rate is small, because E[KL(p(z|x;θ_q^t, θ_d) || p(z|x;θ_q^{t-k}, θ_d))] depends only on query encoder movement against a fixed document manifold — but it becomes provably worse when the optimal retrieval geometry requires co-adaptation of both encoders, as in multi-hop reasoning tasks where document-to-document relevance structure needs to shift alongside query representations. Practical systems like Dragon+ (Lin & Ma, 2023) address this by using progressive document encoder unfreezing — keeping the document encoder frozen for the first N steps to build a stable query-document alignment, then jointly fine-tuning with a much lower document-side learning rate — which approximates an optimal bias-variance tradeoff by ensuring δ_d << δ_q throughout training while still allowing the document manifold to co-adapt slowly.

The invariant that must be preserved is the relative angular order of document embeddings with respect to every query direction in the retrieval cone — formally, for any query embedding q and any pair of documents d_i, d_j in the index, the sign of (q·d_i - q·d_j) must be preserved under the query encoder update, which is equivalent to requiring that the update's induced rotation R on query space does not move any query vector across a hyperplane bisecting any relevant document pair. This is a instance of the order-preserving embedding constraint, and it is related to the Voronoi cell structure of the document index: top-k retrieval is stable if and only if the rotated query R·q remains within the same Voronoi cell (under cosine distance) as the original query q — meaning the maximal angular perturbation tolerable is bounded by the minimum angular width of the Voronoi cell containing q, which for dense retrieval indices over 13M Wikipedia documents is typically on the order of 0.5-2 degrees in high-dimensional space, an extremely tight constraint. Enforcing this invariant directly is computationally intractable for large corpora because it requires maintaining the full Voronoi tessellation of the document embedding space and checking cell membership after every gradient step — the Voronoi diagram in 768 dimensions over 13M points has no tractable exact representation and approximate HNSW or IVF-PQ indices used in practice (Faiss, ScaNN) only approximate these boundaries with recall@100 around 95-98%, meaning small angular drifts near cell boundaries cause retrieval rank flips that the approximation cannot predict. A tractable relaxation is to enforce local isotropy preservation: rather than tracking global Voronoi structure, constrain the query encoder update to lie in the null space of the Jacobian of the retrieval function with respect to query embedding directions that are close (within ε cosine distance) to existing document embeddings — this is the approach implicit in query-side regularization schemes like those in ANCE (Xiong et al., 2021), which use hard negative mining to identify near-boundary query-document pairs and apply contrastive penalties that effectively widen the angular margin around current top-k boundaries. The honest answer is that no deployed system enforces this invariant exactly: ANCE, ColBERT-v2, and Dragon+ all accept some retrieval rank instability during query encoder fine-tuning and compensate through periodic hard negative refresh cycles, treating rank-flip frequency as an empirical hyperparameter rather than a theoretically controlled quantity — which means the stability guarantee is statistical rather than geometric, holding in expectation over the query distribution but failing for individual queries near Voronoi boundaries.

The correct framework is Filippov's theory of differential inclusions, which replaces the discontinuous ODE ẋ = f(x) with a set-valued map ẋ ∈ F(x) where F(x) is the convex hull of all limit values of f in a neighborhood of the discontinuity — applied to the ANCE training dynamics, this means replacing the hard-negative operator H(θ) with its Filippov regularization H̄(θ) = conv(lim_{θ'→θ} H(θ')), which is well-defined even at Voronoi boundaries where H jumps.
